passage: At break in Osaka, Sami saw Kaito sitting alone on the bench by the bike shed with his sleeve pressed to his face. Sami's first thought was to laugh, because Kaito never cried. Instead he stopped a few steps away. He could not tell whether Kaito was hurt, sad, angry or even relieved after the maths test. “Are you okay?” he asked. Kaito shrugged and sniffed. Sami sat down on the far end of the bench and unwrapped his rice ball, saying nothing more. After a while, Kaito wiped his eyes and pushed the bench a little to make room.

qa.q: Where did Sami find Kaito?
qa.a: On the bench by the bike shed.

qa.q: Why did Sami not laugh or guess when he saw Kaito crying?
qa.a: He realised he could not tell if Kaito was hurt, sad, angry or relieved, so he thought asking and staying close would be safer than deciding for him.

qa.q: What did Sami's quiet company do for Kaito?
qa.a: It gave Kaito space without pressure, and later Kaito made room on the bench, which suggests he was starting to feel a little better.

qa.q: What might Kaito have wanted from a classmate who found him crying?
qa.a: He may have wanted someone who did not tease or make him explain right away, and Sami's silence gave him that. 🙂

grounding: A child reads a crying classmate, cannot know the cause, and chooses asking and quiet company over laughing or guessing.

passage: The bell rang for lunch and Yogesh noticed that Swati was still at her desk, wiping her face with her hands. Two boys near the door started to smirk. Yogesh frowned at them and walked over. Swati might have been sad about her lost pencil box, or angry about the group project, or maybe she was just tired. He did not know. He crouched beside her chair. “Are you okay? I can sit here if you want.” Swati nodded a little without looking up. Yogesh took out his own sandwich and waited with her until Ms. Ramanathan came in.

qa.q: Who came over to Swati's desk?
qa.a: Yogesh walked over and crouched beside her chair.

qa.q: What was Yogesh thinking about why Swati was crying?
qa.a: He thought it might be sadness over her pencil box, anger about a group project or simple tiredness, and he admitted to himself that he did not know.

qa.q: Why was Yogesh's approach better than the smirking at the door?
qa.a: He asked and offered to stay, which respects her feelings, while smirking would have added embarrassment to whatever already hurt.

qa.q: How might Swati feel about the two boys and about Yogesh?
qa.a: She might feel exposed by the boys and comforted by Yogesh, since her small nod shows she accepted his company.

grounding: A classmate cries, the cause is uncertain, and the peer asks and stays quietly rather than laughing or guessing.

passage: I'm Nikita. When the scholarship results were read out, Aman put his head down on the desk and his shoulders shook. A couple of boys sniggered. “He didn't get it.” Varun, who sits beside Aman, didn't laugh and didn't guess. He just shifted his chair a bit closer and sat there, quiet, until Aman looked up. Then he asked, “You okay?” Aman wiped his face and laughed shakily. “I got it. I thought I wouldn't. My mum's going to cry too.” Varun grinned and clapped his shoulder. I don't know what Varun was thinking, but he was the only one who got it right.

qa.q: What was read out in class?
qa.a: The scholarship results were read out.

qa.q: What was Aman feeling when his shoulders shook?
qa.a: Aman was overwhelmed with relief and joy at getting the scholarship, not sadness, as the sniggering boys assumed.

qa.q: Why did Varun's approach work better than guessing?
qa.a: He offered quiet company and then asked, which let Aman share the real reason for his tears.

qa.q: How does Nikita view the moment?
qa.a: Nikita sees that the boys guessed wrong, and that only Varun, by waiting and asking, got it right.

grounding: Shows a child reading a crying classmate by offering quiet company and asking, rather than guessing, when the tears were relief.

passage: Monday: After PE, Mahima sat on the steps crying, fists clenched. Himani thought, She's hurt her ankle, and ran for the first-aid box. Mahima pushed it away. “I'm not hurt.” Himani didn't know what to do, so she just sat on the step beside her. After a while Mahima muttered, “They picked everyone except me. Again.” She was angry, not hurt. Wednesday: Himani noticed Mahima eating alone and joined her with her tiffin. They didn't talk about PE, just about a show they both liked. Friday: Himani was a captain. She picked Mahima first. Mahima's eyes shone, and this time nobody needed to ask why.

qa.q: What did Himani run for on Monday?
qa.a: Himani ran for the first-aid box.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling as she cried on the steps?
qa.a: Mahima was angry and hurt at being left out again, not physically injured as Himani first guessed.

qa.q: What did Himani do right after her first guess was wrong?
qa.a: She stopped guessing and simply sat beside Mahima, which gave her space to explain.

qa.q: What would change if Himani had laughed or walked away?
qa.a: Mahima would have been left alone with her anger, and the friendship might never have started.

grounding: Shows a child learning that a classmate's tears can mean anger rather than pain, and quiet company working better than guessing.

passage: Tushar, when your friend cried today, you froze. That's all right. Let your Pema Abi tell you what I learned in Gangtok, long ago. A girl in my class, Dechen, started crying in the middle of the maths lesson. Some laughed. I thought, Her mother must be ill; that was the saddest thing I could imagine. At break I sat beside her, not saying anything, just sharing my momos. After a while I asked, “Are you okay?” She said, “I read the question aloud wrong and everyone laughed. I'm so ashamed.” It wasn't sadness at all. If I had guessed out loud, I'd have made it worse. So I just sat. Sometimes that is enough.

qa.q: Where did young Pema go to school?
qa.a: Pema went to school in Gangtok.

qa.q: What was Dechen feeling as she cried in maths?
qa.a: Dechen felt ashamed and embarrassed after reading the question aloud wrong and being laughed at.

qa.q: What choice did young Pema make, and why did it help?
qa.a: She sat quietly, shared her food and then asked, instead of guessing out loud, which let Dechen say what was wrong.

qa.q: How might Dechen have felt about the classmates who laughed?
qa.a: Dechen probably felt more embarrassed and alone because of their laughter.

grounding: Shows a child reading a crying classmate by offering quiet company and asking, since the cause turned out to be embarrassment.

passage:
Annual Day rehearsal was chaos: drums, a stuck microphone, and Sir shouting that they had ten minutes left in the hall. Indu found Elizabeth behind the stage curtains, crying hard into her sleeve.

Two boys peeked in. "Forgot her lines, probably." "Or someone pinched her." One snickered.

Indu ignored them. She sat down on the dusty floor, not too close, and waited. After a while she asked, "Are you okay? You don't have to say."

Elizabeth wiped her nose. "Mummy just called the office. My grandpa's operation went fine. I've been scared all week." She laughed through the tears. "I don't even know why I'm crying now."

Indu handed her a tissue. "Relief, maybe."

qa.q: Where did Indu find Elizabeth crying?
qa.a: Behind the stage curtains.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth most likely feeling as she cried?
qa.a: Mostly relief after a week of fear about her grandpa's operation, with some leftover worry, not the sadness the boys guessed.

qa.q: Which choice helped Elizabeth open up?
qa.a: Indu sat quietly nearby, waited and asked, "Are you okay? You don't have to say," instead of guessing or laughing.

qa.q: How did the boys read Elizabeth's tears?
qa.a: They guessed forgotten lines or a pinch, and one snickered, with no idea that the tears were really relief.

grounding: It shows a child learning that a crying classmate could be feeling many things, and quiet company and a gentle question working better than guessing.
